final_answer: Best answer, with a verification limitation: neither office has a Guidelines-based advantage over the other, because the Guidelines are the same in both districts and relevant-conduct rules (USSG 1B1.3(a)(2)) aggregate loss from same-course-of-conduct or common-scheme acts regardless of the district or state in which they occurred. The goal of maximum prison time is therefore served by one comprehensive indictment that captures the Georgia and South Carolina claims together, so the loss amount and number of counts are combined in a single Chapter 3/5 computation, rather than two separate prosecutions. Separate indictments by both offices risk the second sentence being run concurrently or reduced by adjustment under USSG 5G1.3 (where the first conviction's conduct is relevant conduct that increased the offense level, 5G1.3(b) requires adjustment/concurrency), and the second court may group or discount. The office that should indict is whichever can establish proper venue over all claims: under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a), an offense committed in more than one district, or a scheme using mail or interstate commerce, may be prosecuted in any district in which it was begun, continued or completed. If the false claims were executed as one scheme and the claims (or the payor/processing of them) touch both districts, either office may bring the unified case; the choice then turns on which district has the larger share of the claims, loss and payor/venue contacts, and on a government-wide coordination decision. If the two states' claims are factually separate schemes with no venue link, each office can charge only its own claims and the maximum total comes from two prosecutions with the second sentence run consecutively (permitted under 5G1.3(d) 'in any other case') but not required. Statutory ceiling per 1347 count is 10 years (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death), and multiple counts can be stacked under 5G1.2(d) when the guideline range exceeds the statutory maximum of a single count.
